Sources and methods

How to read the atlas

A research record of land-border closures and restrictions between 21 October 2016 and 21 October 2026. It describes past events, not whether a crossing is open today.

What is included?

Restrictions at land borders and international river ferries, including short closures. A record may concern one crossing, several crossings or a wider policy, and may contain several stages as the rules changed.

Routine overnight hours, individual visa refusals, checks that still allow passage, and air- or sea-only restrictions are outside this dataset. Related records can describe parts of the same event.

What do the lines mean?

Colour shows the recorded reason for a restriction. A solid line means the selected evidence explicitly describes border-wide scope. A dotted line means the restriction concerns particular crossings, a smaller area, or an extent that remains unclear. If records are mixed, the line stays dotted.

Both styles locate the relevant border; neither traces the exact closed section or means that every traveller was stopped. Read the description for the affected crossings, people, goods and exceptions. A border without colour may simply lack collected evidence.

What do the dates mean?

Observed closure: sources describe an interruption to passage. Policy in force: the dates refer to a rule, without proving continuous closure on the ground. Announced closure dates: a planned schedule whose implementation is not confirmed. Repeated closures: a period containing closures and possible openings.

Some records have only dated reports or disputed dates. These appear on those dates, without filling the gaps between them. A last report, scheduled end or change in law is not automatically a reopening. Missing end dates are not extended to the present.

Days are differences between calendar dates, not measured hours. A same-day event is not counted as a full day. Overlapping stages must not be added together.

How should I use the timeline?

Border restrictions shows records with evidence in the selected month. It does not mean the restriction lasted throughout that month. Closures beginning shows supported starting months. All recorded closures includes records without dates.

Typing in search switches to all recorded closures so that a date filter does not hide a matching event. You can then narrow the dates yourself.

What is a coded rationale?

A category summarises a reason attributed by a source. A record can have several categories because reasons, actors or stages differ. An official explanation is not proof of the complete motive. Grey means no category is assigned; the reason may be unknown or fall outside the categories.

Counts describe the records collected, not how often closures occur worldwide. Continental and rationale totals can overlap. The duration charts use a smaller group with sufficiently clear dates and reopening evidence, and show its coverage alongside the comparison.

Where can I check the evidence?

Open a record for a plain summary, dated stages and named source links. Further details contain the qualifications and review history. Later corrections take precedence over original claims, which are labelled as historical.

Read all records opens a wider reading view. Download CSV saves every matching record, including those beyond the first page. Analysis offers chart data, chronology and review downloads. Save view downloads the current map and its key.

Some evidence was available in full; some only as extracts. Several reports can repeat one original account, so more links do not necessarily mean independent confirmation.
